titleStmt.title: Therapeutic options for the management of abnormal uterine bleeding

analytic.title: Therapeutic options for the management of abnormal uterine bleeding

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Just as the investigation of abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB) is approached systematically using the two FIGO systems for AUB in the reproductive years, treatment options can be considered similarly. Therapeutic options fall into two categories-medical and surgical-and while medical management is typically regarded as first-line therapy, there are several exceptions defined by the presenting cause or causes, mainly when infertility is a concurrent issue. In the early 1990s, up to 60% of women underwent a hysterectomy for the symptom of heavy menstrual bleeding (HMB), but this figure has decreased. In 2014, 37.3% of women seen in secondary care in the UK underwent some sort of surgical intervention [1]. The number of women undergoing a hysterectomy for benign disorders continues to decline, along with an increase in hysterectomies performed using minimally invasive techniques. Discussions about therapeutic options are tailored to the individual patient, and we include the risks and benefits of each option, including no management, to enable the patient to make an informed choice. The different types of treatment options and the factors affecting decision-making are considered in this article.

div.head: Introduction [heading numbering has been added per IJGO style. Please check that this has been done correctly]
div.p: Therapeutic options for abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB) are either medical or procedural, with medical management typically first-line therapy [2,3]. Identification of the specific cause of or contributors to the AUB symptoms is crucial to the identification of appropriate therapeutic options; a process that is the subject of FIGO's two AUB systems [4] (and which has been described elsewhere in this Supplement (Int REF Jain et al.). Based on this assessment, decisions about therapeutic options, including expectant management, should be tailored to the individual patient, including a discussion of the risks and benefits of each, enabling them to make an informed choice. Whereas this article refers to women, the concepts apply to all menstruating people. We start with an overview of the types of procedural and medical interventions that may be used to treat one or more of the causes of AUB in the reproductive years, and then discuss how they may be applied to the various aspects of diagnoses categorized in FIGO's System 2: the PALM-COEIN system. Treatment of the oftenassociated iron deficiency is not discussed here but is the subject of another paper in this Supplement (Int REF Auerbach).

div.head: Procedural interventions
div.p: In the early 1990s, up to 60% of women underwent a hysterectomy for the management of the symptom of heavy menstrual bleeding (HMB) [5]. However, with advances in medical and procedural options, many of which can be performed in an office or outpatient facility, hysterectomy is no longer the mainstay of treatment.

div.head: Hysterectomy
div.p: Hysterectomy is one of the most common gynecological surgical procedures worldwide [6]. It is performed vaginally or abdominally, the latter via laparotomy or laparoscopically, with or without remote microprocessor-based assistance [7]. A 2015 Cochrane review concluded that, where possible, a vaginal approach should be chosen over the abdominal route in hysterectomy for benign disorders [8]. Where vaginal hysterectomy is not possible, both a laparoscopic approach and abdominal hysterectomy have their pros and cons and these should be incorporated in the decision-making process. [8]. The laparoscopic route has been increasingly used; in 2017, an English study found that 47.2% of procedures were performed laparoscopically, compared with 46.5% via laparotomy [9]. This will however depend on the skill of the surgeon and the size of the uterus. While hysterectomy is highly effective for treating AUB symptoms, with a high satisfaction rate at 3 years [10], it has many risks including hemorrhage, infection, venous thromboembolism, and injury to surrounding structures, including ureters and bowel [7,11]. The overall complication rate is 4.4% for laparoscopic hysterectomy and 4.9% when hysterectomy is performed via laparotomy [11]. Depending on the surgical approach, full recovery from a hysterectomy may require several weeks and, of course, it is inappropriate for women who wish to preserve their fertility.

div.head: Intrauterine surgery
div.p: Surgery performed within the endometrial cavity, and cervical canal, can be accomplished under hysteroscopic direction or with various specially designed devices, particularly for endometrial ablation.

div.head: Endometrial ablation
div.p: The process of destroying the endometrial layer (endometrial ablation) to treat the symptom of HMB dates to the late 19th century, with published techniques reported through the 20th century and subject to extensive review [12][13][14]. In the latter part of the 20th century, several techniques were developed [Editing OK?] that used laser and, more often, radiofrequency electrical energy via a modified urological resectoscope to ablate, vaporize, or resect the endometrial tissue; hence the term resectoscopic endometrial ablation or REA. By the beginning of the 21st century, the concept of nonresectoscopic endometrial ablation (NREA) was revived, with the introduction of several devices that employ a variety of hyperthermic or hypothermic techniques to replicate what was achieved under hysteroscopic direction. The rationale for developing these systems was some combination of reduction of the risks associated with REA, and the potential to perform these procedures in a less resource-intense setting, potentially under local anesthesia. Currently, NREA techniques are widely used in preference to REA and have been demonstrated to be generally effective alternatives to hysterectomy for the treatment of HMB for women not desiring pregnancy in the future [15].

There are, perhaps, some unfortunate descriptions of endometrial ablation in general and the NREA systems in particular. First, they are often mislabeled as first-and second-generation techniques, when NREA was first published almost 100 years before the introduction of REA. More importantly, the term global endometrial ablation (GEA) is often used, even though no system comes close to the predictable attainment of amenorrhea [15][16][17].

div.head: Hysteroscopic removal of structural lesions
div.p: Hysteroscopically guided systems designed to transect, dissect, vaporize, morcellate, and remove structural lesions that can cause AUB are minimally invasive and can be employed to treat symptoms and retain or restore fertility. The original and perhaps most versatile system is the radiofrequency resectoscope-the same one used for resectoscopic endometrial ablation. The surgeon passes the instrument through the cervix, visualizes and distends the endometrial cavity with fluid media, and then uses a radiofrequency loop electrode to resect the lesion, morcellating and removing it with serial passes. More recent has been the development of hysteroscopically guided systems that can be used to morcellate tissue mechanically or electromechanically via an oscillating blade within a hollow metal cannula that, by its connection to a remote suction apparatus and tissue trap, allows for simultaneous aspiration of the fragmented specimen.

Smaller lesions, such as polyps, can be removed with more simply designed instruments passed through the operating channel of a hysteroscopic system. These devices comprise scissors, narrow-caliber radiofrequency needles, and grasping and biopsy forceps that can be used to transect, bivalve, and dissect targeted tissue.
Scissors or blunt dissecting instruments may be necessary to facilitate the removal of deeper Type 1 and Type 2 leiomyomas, ideally by dissecting within the pseudocapsule [18].

While minimally invasive and frequently compatible with office, clinic, or surgery center use, often with only local anesthesia, there are still potential complications of these procedures. These include perforation, hemorrhage, and absorption of excess distension media, which can cause some combination of fluid overload and hyponatremia and its related consequences depending on the media used. This means that these procedures should be performed by well-trained surgeons operating with the appropriate equipment in the context of centers with the resources required to minimize risk and to rapidly and effectively respond to adverse events.

div.head: Uterine-conserving abdominal surgery
div.p: When myomectomy is necessary to treat AUB, and if hysteroscopic myomectomy is not feasible, the procedure may be accomplished via laparotomy or, preferably, laparoscopic techniques, including those assisted by microprocessor-based remotely activated devices often called robots. Less commonly, such approaches may be used to remove adenomyosis, although the indications and appropriate patient selection are less well evolved. These procedures will be dealt with in more detail in the later sections on adenomyosis (AUB-A) and leiomyoma (AUB-L) [Editing OK?].

div.head: Image-guided procedures
div.p: Image-guided techniques were developed initially for leiomyoma symptoms but have also been applied to treat adenomyosis. The imaging component may be ultrasound, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), fluoroscopy with contrast, or even laparoscopy, and the approaches to treating the target tissue include vascular occlusion and hyperthermic techniques such as high-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU) and radiofrequency electrical energy.

div.head: Hyperthermic ablation
div.p: Hyperthermic ablation involves the application of thermal energy to abnormal tissue, causing the intracellular temperature to rise to the point where cellular death occurs [19,20]. There are three energy sources that may be used for hyperthermic ablation: radiofrequency, microwave, and HIFU [21].

Radiofrequency ablation (RFA) uses probes tipped with electrodes that deliver highfrequency electrical energy to the tissue under laparoscopic and laparoscopic ultrasound direction [22] or transcervically utilizing the guidance provided by transvaginal ultrasound [23]. Microwave ablation involves the insertion of a microwave probe transcutaneously into the target under ultrasound guidance [24], after which microwave energy is applied to destroy tissue. In contrast, HIFU does not require the insertion of a probe; instead, it is delivered transabdominally and targeted most often by MRI, although ultrasound-guided systems are available in some countries [25].

div.head: Uterine artery embolization
div.p: Uterine artery embolization (UAE) is an interventional radiological procedure that, after the institution of intravenous conscious sedation, starts with catheterization of the uterine arteries, usually via the right femoral artery as directed by fluoroscopy.

Each uterine artery is occluded with gel or, more commonly, permanent microscopic embolic spheres or ovules until there is no longer any fluoroscopically visualized flow to the uterus. The uterus undergoes a period of ischemia until collateral flow, principally from the ovarian vessels, re-establishes vascularization. Patients are typically discharged home the same or the next day, depending on the amount of pain experienced. The therapeutic effect, at least for leiomyomas, is based on the leiomyoma's heightened susceptibility to ischemia related to its tenuous blood supply; the myometrium is quite resistant because of its abundant collateral circulation.

There is some concern regarding the risk for decreased ovarian function following UAE due to misembolization of the ovarian artery-an adverse event that now appears to be less common than initially thought [26]. Recent meta-analyses have suggested no appreciable impact on ovarian reserve as measured by mean serum concentrations of anti-Müllerian and follicle-stimulating hormones [27,28]. The issues regarding UAE and both fertility and future pregnancy remain the prevailing concerns about the propriety of this procedure in women wishing to conceive in the future [29][30][31].

div.head: Medical interventions
div.p: Medical management is commonly the first-line treatment option for most causes of AUB. It comprises a spectrum of formulations and methods of administration and is an attractive option for those wishing to maintain fertility. It may be used to provide symptom relief while an investigation of the underlying cause of AUB is underway.

This may be a short-term treatment to induce amenorrhea to allow for correction of anemia and restoration of iron stores before surgery or more definitive treatment options. It may also be used as a longer-term intervention to control symptoms, especially HMB if the patient is either unsuitable for or does not desire a surgical intervention. The available medical treatment options for AUB in the reproductive years are summarized in Table 1.

div.head: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatories
div.p: Several nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) options are available, including mefenamic acid, naproxen, naproxen sodium, ibuprofen, and diclofenac. They work at the endometrium level, reducing prostaglandin levels by inhibiting the cyclo-oxygenase (COX) enzyme-the reason they are also referred to as COX inhibitors [32]. Given only during menstruation, NSAIDs are suitable options for women wishing to conceive, have a beneficial effect on dysmenorrhea [32], and reduce blood loss by 25%-35% in up to 75% of women [33]. A recent Cochrane review found them to be more effective than placebo but less effective than tranexamic acid or the levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system (LNG-IUS), and that there was no difference between different NSAIDs in their effect on HMB [32]. They are generally well tolerated but are contraindicated in women with underlying bleeding disorders, gastric ulceration, or kidney disease [34].

div.head: Tranexamic acid
div.p: Tranexamic acid is an antifibrinolytic agent that prevents fibrinolysis by reversibly blocking plasminogen [35]. There are a number of oral formulations, with doses ranging from 1000 mg to 1300 mg 3-4 times per day. It may be used on its own or with an NSAID during days 1-5 of the menstrual cycle if there are no contraindications [2,36]. Tranexamic acid has been shown to reduce menstrual blood loss by 26%-50% and is more effective than NSAIDs alone [35], but it has minimal effect on dysmenorrhea [37]. It is generally well tolerated and has few adverse effects [35]; there is no evidence that it increases the risk of thromboembolic events, even in patients at high risk [38,39].

div.head: Hormonal therapy
div.p: The use of medications that suppress or otherwise manipulate gonadal steroid activity on the endometrium or disorders in the myometrium, such as adenomyosis and leiomyomas, has a major place in the management of AUB in the reproductive years. Such approaches comprise the pharmacologic administration of gonadal steroid-containing formulations, or the use of agents that indirectly impact gonadal steroid production or activity such as progesterone receptor or gonadotropin modulators.

div.head: Levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine systems
div.p: For those not planning immediate pregnancy and experiencing AUB manifestations such as HMB and dysmenorrhea from several potential causes, the 52-mg levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system (52-mg LNG-IUS) is considered first-line by many [2]. Its mechanism of action is to suppress endometrial activity by the continuous local release of low dose levonorgestrel. The system is fertility sparing, provides reliable contraception, has a robust evidence base, and appears to be more effective, with a lower adverse effect profile, than oral progestin-based hormonal therapy [2,36,[40][41][42][43]. For those with the symptom of HMB thought to reflect endometrial AUB (AUB-E) [Editing OK?], compared with endometrial ablation, there are similar rates of reduction of menstrual blood loss and level of patient [Wording missing? Please clarify meaning] [43,44].

Patients should be counselled that substantially reduced bleeding volume is typically experienced in the first postinsertion menses [45,46] and further reduction may occur for up to 6 months [2,36]. Studies show it has the potential to decrease blood loss by up to 96% [36], and 5.2%-18.2% of women report amenorrhea at 1 year [47,48]. Intermenstrual spotting is common initially but reduces to about 25% of users at 6 months after insertion with progressive reduction for up to 3 years after insertion [42,49]. It is better tolerated than oral progestins [41] and has a more significant beneficial effect on quality of life and HMB volume when compared with other medical therapy [43]. Common reasons for discontinuing treatment are treatment failure and prolonged or irregular bleeding [50]. The 52-mg LNG-IUS is approved for up to 5 years for HMB [51,52], the 19.5-mg LNG-IUS for 5 years for contraceptive purposes, and the 13.5-mg LNG-IUS is licensed for 3 years as contraception [52]; neither the 19.5-mg nor 13.5-mg versions have been evaluated for the symptom of HMB [53]. The LNG-IUS is widely available in high-income countries. However, access is limited in some low-and middle-income countries (LMICs) except in the private sector [54] due to several factors, including cost and a lack of trained providers [54].

div.head: Combined estrogen and progestin formulations
div.p: Estrogens and progestins can be given together in several forms, as combined hormonal contraception, including as a pill, vaginal ring, or patch. When given cyclically, all have been shown to regulate the menstrual cycle and reduce the volume of menstrual bleeding [55]. Several different preparations are available, with the differences being the dose of estrogen and the dose and type of progestin [56].
Their mechanism of action is through inhibition of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), improving the stability of the endometrium and causing endometrial atrophy [55].
Combined estrogen and progestin is less effective than the 52-mg LNG-IUS but has been shown to reduce blood loss by 12%-77% compared to placebo [55].

Combined hormonal contraceptives can be considered providing there are no contraindications [2,57]. They are typically given for 21 days, followed by a pill-, patch-, or ring-free week during which a withdrawal bleed occurs. They can also be tricycled, where three packets are taken consecutively without the pill-, patch-, or ring-free week to reduce the number of withdrawal bleeds that occur. Furthermore, some women will be given them continuously [36,56]. Indeed, there is no medical rationale for any discontinuation-a circumstance that should allow clinicians to use these products in a continuous fashion. The ring has the advantage that the dose of systemic estrogen is half that of the pill or patch [30]. Combined hormonal contraceptives are often well tolerated; however, there are several clinical circumstances, such as existing vascular disease, smoking over the age of 35, or a previous estrogen-responsive malignancy, where their use is relatively or absolutely contraindicated [58].They are, however, suitable for most women.

div.head: Other progestins
div.p: Where estrogen-containing formulations are contraindicated, single-agent progestogens may provide a viable option for some causes of AUB. There are several formulations and administration schedules, and some have been evaluated to determine their ability to provide symptom control [2,36]. Noncontraceptive oral progestin therapy is given for 21 days each month [41], and there is no evidence of benefit to women when it is given just in the luteal phase of those with regular menstrual cycles suggesting ovulation [36,57]. The most commonly reported regimen is norethisterone 5 mg, three times a day, on days 5-26 of the menstrual cycle [36]. This has been shown to reduce menstrual loss by up to 80%, but it has a high incidence of progestogenic adverse effects [36]. A somewhat unique progestin is dienogest, an orally administered agent with continuous administration, which is particularly effective in the treatment of AUB-A and related symptoms [59]; however, it is not widely available in all countries [Editing OK?].

Continuous injectable or implantable progestogens have also been evaluated for the management of some causes of AUB [36,57]. Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate is widely used as a contraceptive agent and is administered every 3 months via either the intramuscular or subcutaneous route [36]. Up to half will experience amenorrhea after 1 year of use [36,57], although irregular bleeding is a common initial adverse effect, particularly in the first year [28]. Users may experience a temporary reduction in bone mineral density with prolonged use (beyond 2 years) and some studies have shown an increased fracture risk among some specific user subgroups [60,61].

div.head: Gonadotropin-releasing hormone modulators
div.p: Hypothalamic control of gonadotropins produced in the pituitary is via gonadotropinreleasing hormone (GnRH). By effectively turning off GnRH, the ovarian production of estradiol and progesterone is effectively stopped, creating a temporary menopausal state that can be exploited to treat a number of gonadal steroidresponsive disorders, including many of the causes of AUB in the reproductive years.

div.head: GnRH agonists
div.p: GnRH agonists are decapeptides, similar in structure to GnRH, which competitively bind to GnRH receptors and are administered by subcutaneous or intramuscular injection. With continuous (as opposed to pulsatile) administration, there is an initial flare of gonadotropin release and then, in about 3-4 weeks, downregulation of the release of FSH and luteinizing hormone (LH); examples include goserelin and leuprorelin. This flare can lead to a heavy bleed experienced in the first two2-3 weeks after administration, which is undesirable in individuals with already compromised iron status. Although careful counselling before starting treatment can mitigate the impact on the patient, some prescribe progestogens for the first month of treatment.

The ultimate downregulation of gonadotropins leads to a dramatic reduction in the ovarian production of estrogen, which, in turn, eliminates progesterone as well. This mechanism of action leads to significant hypoestrogenic adverse effects, including loss of bone mineral density when GnRH agonists are used alone for more than 6 months. However, this risk can be mitigated using add-back therapy [62]. In view of this, they are often only considered as a stand-alone treatment where surgical management, including hysterectomy, is unsuitable or unacceptable to a patient, and other medical treatments have failed [63]. They may also be used prior to fertility treatment to improve the chance of a successful pregnancy [63], or as adjunctive therapy before hysterectomy [64].

div.head: GnRH antagonists
div.p: GnRH antagonists competitively bind with GnRH receptors causing an immediate suppression of gonadotropin release and, with sufficient dosing, rapidly leading to a reversible menopausal state [64]. A perceived advantage of GnRH antagonists, compared with GnRH agonists, is their capacity for oral administration, avoiding the need for injections. Further, is the lack of the initial GnRH agonist-induced estradiol flare, thus eliminating the risk of a heavy bleed in the first month of use [65].

There are now three orally administered GnRH antagonists variously available around the world: elagolix, relugolix, and linzagolix. These are available in several dosages and, in some instances, combined with ethinyl estradiol and norethindrone acetate add-back regimens [Editing OK?] to mitigate the otherwise undesirable vasomotor symptoms and loss of trabecular bone secondary to hypoestrogenemia.
Formulations with or without add-back estrogen and progestin have been demonstrated effective for treating leiomyoma-associated HMB and are currently approved for up to 2 years of use [66][67][68].

For extended use, all likely require replacement doses of estrogen and progestin, not only for vasomotor symptoms but also to prevent vaginal atrophy and the adverse bone effects of osteopenia and osteoporosis.

div.head: Selective progesterone receptor modulators
div.p: Selective progesterone receptor modulators (SPRMs) are synthetic steroids that act by combining with the progesterone receptor. They are called selective because they combine only to a small degree with other receptors, such as glucocorticoid receptors, which could lead to potential adverse effects [69]. Their primary use has been treatment of symptomatic fibroids due to their proapoptotic and antiproliferative effects [69], although studies are ongoing to evaluate their use in other causes of AUB [70]. They are highly effective in reducing menstrual blood loss, decrease the size of the fibroids, and are very well tolerated [71].

The most commonly used SPRM is ulipristal acetate. It has been shown to be as effective as GnRH analogues in reducing uterine bleeding but with a lower adverse effect profile [69], and can be used as adjunctive therapy to reduce the size of fibroids before myomectomy [69]. Unfortunately, their use has been limited after hearings at the European Medicines Agency in 2018 and 2019 due to rare but sometimes significant problems with liver disease [69,70]. New progesterone receptor modulators are being investigated and clinical trials are underway, but whether other drugs in this class will receive approval remains to be seen.

div.head: Polyp (AUB-P)
div.p: Polyps may be cervical or endometrial and are often asymptomatic [72]. Endometrial polyps are frequently found in association with AUB (24%-41%), but by far, the most common symptom is intermenstrual bleeding [72]. As a result, an association of the symptom of HMB with the finding of endometrial polyps should be made with caution; there is generally another explanation. The overall risk of malignancy in the polyps found in premenopausal women is 1.12% [73], with symptomatic women at increased risk [73]. Although polyps found in premenopausal women have a low risk of malignancy [74][75][76], it is recommended that they are removed when symptomatic, both for the treatment of symptoms and histologic examination [74,75].
Historically, polyps were blindly avulsed [74], but recurrence is common, making hysteroscopically directed removal the recommended approach [74,75,77].

Hysteroscopic polypectomy is safe and effective, acceptable to most women using no or local anesthesia, and has a low rate of recurrence [74,75,77]. The choice of surgical technique depends on the size and site of the polyp, the operator's skill and experience, and the available equipment and facilities [74].

With appropriate patient selection, the excision of small polyps (<2 cm) can be performed in an outpatient setting with the patient awake [75,77]. It is often possible to resect small polyps in one piece; bipolar radiofrequency needles, scissors, or crocodile forceps are instruments that may be used to accomplish this aim [74,75].

Polyps greater than 2 cm require morcellation, with a longer operating time; depending on the surgeon, available equipment, polyp size, and patient choice, this may require performance in an institutional environment [74,75]. The gold standard technique for polyps larger than 2 cm is hysteroscopic loop excision [75]; however, newer devices, such as manual or electromechanical morcellation systems, are increasingly used [75].

div.head: Adenomyosis (AUB-A)
div.p: Adenomyosis is defined as the existence of endometrium-like glands and stroma in the myometrium, typically surrounded by smooth muscle hyperplasia and hypertrophy [78]. While the pathogenesis is still poorly understood, it may include congenital or acquired extension into the myometrium from the endometrium, invasion from external endometriosis, and derivation from either embryonic or adult stem cells [79]. The prevalence of adenomyosis in AUB is unclear but has been estimated to be 20%-35% [80].

In the past, hysterectomy was the only available and effective treatment for adenomyosis [19]. However, medical management and image-guided techniques can now be used successfully in many instances and depending on the patient's current and future goals regarding pregnancy.

div.head: Medical management [Please check that the added numbering is correct here and on]
div.p: If AUB-A is diagnosed, the choice of medical management will depend on several factors, including the presenting symptoms (HMB with or without dysmenorrhea), responses to previous therapy, uterine volume, and the short and intermediate goals for fertility, including the presence of infertility. There may also be barriers to access related to the jurisdictional approval process and the cost of the pharmaceutical interventions themselves. It should also be recognized that the adenomyosis visualized by imaging may not be responsible for the AUB, in particular, HMB symptoms. Evidence from the UK has demonstrated that bleeding volume is typically normal when there is only a single ultrasound-defined adenomyosis feature [81].

Evidence of efficacy in the treatment of AUB-A with daily administration of 5 mg norethindrone acetate has been shown [82] and for continuously administered combined estrogen and progestin-containing oral contraceptives [83]-interventions that should be available universally. The oral progestin dienogest is currently approved only in Japan for the treatment of AUB-A with or without dysmenorrhea and, with a daily dose of 2 mg orally, has been shown effective for long-term use provided the uterine fundus is not more than 10 cm in diameter [59]. Another progestin-based approach to treating women with AUB-A and related symptoms is the 52-mg LNG-IUS, which has been demonstrated highly effective in both wellconstructed prospective cohort studies [84] and randomized trials [83,85].

Given their mechanism of action, it is anticipated that both GnRH agonists and antagonists should be efficacious in treating AUB-A, particularly in patients who do not or who no longer respond to progestin-based regimens. Indeed, there is evidence that GnRH agonists can be used effectively, including in a strategy designed to initiate a response, with subsequent chronic management with oral dienogest [86]. There is unsurprising early evidence that GnRH antagonists may be effective for adenomyosis-associated AUB [87,88].
As with all aspects of adenomyosis, more evidence will be necessary before we have clarity regarding matching disease phenotype to the most appropriate medical interventions.

div.head: Image-guided therapy
div.p: Image-guided techniques for treating adenomyosis using ultrasound, MRI, or angiography have been explored with a growing body of evidence supporting safety and efficacy.

div.head: Hyperthermic ablation
div.p: Evidence suggests that all three methods are safe, with few significant adverse effects reported [21], and been shown to reduce dysmenorrhea and HMB in women with adenomyosis [21,25]. Radiofrequency ablation and microwave ablation require a shorter ablation time than HIFU and have been shown to cause a more significant reduction in uterine volume [25].

All three methods [Editing OK?] can be used on their own or in conjunction with the LNG-IUS and/or GnRH agonists [19,20,24]; this combined approach may have superior outcomes [20,21,24,89,90]. Although increasingly used, hyperthermic ablation still has limited availability worldwide [19]. Data demonstrating an effect on future fertility and pregnancy outcomes are currently insufficient, and more research is needed [20,21,23,25].

div.head: Uterine artery embolization
div.p: Uterine artery embolization is increasingly being considered as a uterine-sparing option for adenomyosis [20]. Studies have shown promising results, with improvements reported in dysmenorrhea and blood loss; however, data on the effect of UAE on fertility are still lacking [19,20]. A recent meta-analysis concluded that 82% of patients undergoing UAE avoided a hysterectomy, and quality of life and symptom severity were improved at the 3-month and 7-year follow up [91]. The QUESTA trial (Quality of Life after Embolization vs Hysterectomy in Adenomyosis) is currently being carried out to investigate the use of UAE in the treatment of adenomyosis [92].

div.head: Surgical excision
div.p: Uterine-sparing resection, often called adenomyomectomy, involves excising adenomyotic tissue with the required degree of subsequent myometrial repair. This can range from local excisions similar in scope to myomectomy to extensive resection followed by complex uterine reconstruction [20,63]. Several techniques have been described [19,63], with the majority performed by laparotomy, but laparoscopically directed excision may be an option, especially for relatively welldefined localized lesions [63]. Resection has been shown to reduce bleeding and improve pain and may be used in conjunction with the LNG-IUS or GnRH agonists [20]. A significant consideration, however, is the risk of uterine rupture and complications in subsequent pregnancies [19,63]. A recent systematic review reported that rates of uterine rupture in the next pregnancy are related to the extent of the adenomyosis before surgery, with a rate of uterine rupture for women with diffuse disease of 6.8% versus 0% for women with focal disease [93].

Hysterectomy has historically been the primary treatment option for adenomyosis, but it is now indicated where alternative, more conservative treatment has failed [20] or if it is the only acceptable option for a given patient.

div.head: General considerations
div.p: Uterine leiomyomas, frequently called fibroids, are the most common tumor in women of reproductive age and are often associated with HMB, abdominal discomfort, subfertility, and reduced quality of life. It is probable that submucous fibroids contribute to AUB and infertility [94] while the relationship of intramural fibroids (Type 4 and greater) is less clear [93][94][95]; it is generally accepted that such tumors generally do not affect fertility and have no impact on the frequency, regularity, duration, or volume of menstrual bleeding. Consequently, when leiomyomas not in contact with the endometrium are identified in the context of evaluation of women with AUB (AUBO), the cause of the bleeding likely lies elsewhere (for example, AUB-C, AUB-O, or AUB-E) and therapy directed at the leiomyomas is not likely to be effective (except hysterectomy). In the presence of submucous leiomyomas, women with AUB may be offered medical, traditional surgical, and image-guided procedural interventions depending on the individual patient and considering a number of factors, including their immediate and long-term goals for fertility. For Types 0, 1, and some relatively small-volume Type 2 tumors, hysteroscopic myomectomy is highly effective and safe. In many instances it can even be performed in a clinic or office procedure room [96]. In such circumstances hysteroscopic myomectomy is a compelling choice, almost regardless of the shortor long-term goals of the patient with AUB.

div.head: Medical therapy
div.p: The selection of medical therapy options for women with AUB-L is based on the leiomyoma phenotype and, in part, on the associated symptoms that often include pressure on the surrounding organs and other structures. For example, for a 42year-old woman with the symptom of HMB, not interested in fertility, and a Type 2-5 leiomyoma not amenable to hysteroscopic resection but not causing pressure symptoms, treatment can be focused on the bleeding alone. On the other hand, for a 51-year-old with AUB-LSM and a deep Type 2 leiomyoma but with multiple other leiomyomas enlarging the uterus to the point of causing substantial pressure symptoms, the ideal approach is designed to address both the bleeding and large uterine volume. For those with coincidental infertility, medical therapy is more likely to be an adjunct to myomectomy, if indicated, to reduce myoma and uterine volume and to facilitate the restoration of iron balance if there is coexisting iron deficiency, including iron deficiency anemia. These considerations can lead to a divergent variety of interventions. An individual with a Type 2-5 leiomyoma may respond well to tranexamic acid or contraceptive steroids, including the 52-mg LNG-IUS. On the other hand, an individual with AUB-LSM but with pressure symptoms is more likely to require one of the GnRH modulators to treat both symptoms, with add-back estrogen and progestin if the plan is to use the therapy to bridge to menopause.

div.head: Procedural interventions
div.p: For patients who are not appropriate for or who do not respond satisfactorily to medical treatment, there are several procedural interventions available, depending on the leiomyoma phenotype and the current and future desires regarding pregnancy. Surgery, either myomectomy or hysterectomy, has traditionally been the primary approach for managing symptomatic leiomyoma if medical management is ineffective. However, in addition to myomectomy, the spectrum of image-guided procedures has been applied to the treatment of women with leiomyomas, focusing on AUB symptoms and the impact on myoma volume.
Both myomectomy and UAE have been demonstrated to be effective treatments for improving the quality of life for women with symptomatic fleiomyomas [26,[97][98][99][100].

However, there is a paucity of data regarding the propriety of image-guided interventions, including UAE, on pregnancy rates and outcomes; they may not be appropriate for women with infertility or those desiring future pregnancy [29][30][31].

Available data from China suggest that, for example, comparing myomectomy and UAE, the frequency of repeat interventions was similar, and, at 5 years, an equal proportion of women would recommend their procedure after years [Wording missing? Please clarify meaning] [97,100]. Consequently, all women, including those desiring a future pregnancy, should have the best available evidence before deciding.

div.head: Myomectomy
div.p: When submucous leiomyomas are amenable to hysteroscopically directed removal, such an approach should be high on the list of options, particularly if fertility is an issue. When the leiomyoma phenotype is not amenable to hysteroscopic surgery, an abdominal approach to myomectomy should be offered, performed laparoscopically, if possible, but only if it is thought to provide optimal fertility outcomes. It should be recognized that intrauterine adhesions may be a consequence of submucous myomectomy, particularly when two or more proximal lesions are removed at the same procedure [101][102][103]. As a result, strategies to minimize the risk of such an adverse outcome should be considered, from staging hysteroscopic myomectomy into multiple procedures when there are numerous lesions, to using adhesion barriers, to performing second-look hysteroscopy, at least in high-risk situations.

div.head: Image-guided procedures
div.p: In addition to UAE, other image-guided, minimally invasive interventions can be used to treat fibroids. However, as with UAE, the impact of these ablative therapies on fertility or subsequent pregnancy is generally unclear. Consequently, myomectomy remains the procedure of choice for those with infertility or who otherwise desire future pregnancy.

There is accumulating evidence on radiofrequency ablation (RFA) techniques, with a number showing sustained efficacy in reducing HMB symptoms and leiomyoma volume [104]. There is also an increasing body of evidence describing pregnancy outcomes following RFA, suggesting cautious optimism that adverse events may be relatively low [105]. Transcervical ultrasound-guided RFA with the Sonata system has significantly improved menstrual blood loss for up to 2 years after the procedure [106]. Laparoscopic and simultaneous laparoscopic ultrasound-directed RFA has undergone relatively extensive studies showing enduring HMB results at 3 years [107], and evidence that the approach may be readily adapted to practice [108].

Magnetic resonance-guided focused ultrasound (MRgFUS) has been associated with short-term efficacy; however, long-term outcomes, including the effect on fertility, remain unclear [109]. Early studies of microwave ablation have shown promising results for both safety and efficacy, but more extensive and comparative studies will be needed [110,111].

As a result of the accumulating data on efficacy, national and international guidelines now consider that UAE is considered alongside surgical and medical management. However, it is recognized that the evidence for fertility and pregnancy outcomes after UAE and myomectomy is limited, preventing evidence-based recommendations for women with fibroids wishing to preserve fertility [112,113].

div.head: Malignancy (AUB-M)
div.p: As discussed elsewhere in this Supplement, AUB-M comprises women with AUB in the reproductive years with either endometrial cancer or endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia (EIN), previously known as atypical endometrial hyperplasia (Int REF Jain et al.) Although relatively uncommon in premenopausal women, endometrial cancer is the most common gynecologic cancer in high-resource [Changed from "developed" per IJGO style: OK?] countries, with the incidence rising due to factors such as increasing rates of obesity and delayed pregnancy [114].

In the reproductive years, some individuals with EIN, and even a few highly selected women with endometrial cancer thought to be confined to the endometrium may be appropriate candidates for fertility-sparing, progestin-based therapy with one or a combination of the 52-mg LNG-IUS and continuous, oral progestins such as medroxyprogesterone acetate or megestrol acetate therapy [115]. Pregnancy outcomes are promising with assisted reproductive technologies [116], although pregnancy rates are still only about 20% [117]. Following the desired number of pregnancies, should they occur, the high rate [of what? Please clarify] mandates close surveillance with prophylactic hysterectomy a frequent recommendation.

Both the UK-based Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists and the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists have comprehensive management guidance [115,118]. A detailed description of the management of gynecologic malignancy is outside the scope of this article.

div.head: Coagulopathy (AUB-C)
div.p: Screening and diagnosis of coagulopathies are discussed elsewhere in this Supplement (Int REF Jain et al.). The management of girls and women with AUB-C will generally take place in association with the care of a hematologist, and the specifics of the interventions will vary according to the cause and severity of the coagulopathy. As with other causes, medical management is divided into hormonal and nonhormonal treatment options, which may be used together [119].

Nonhormonal options include antifibrinolytics and desmopressin, which may be given in combination or separately. Tranexamic acid is effective and administered at the start of menstruation in an oral dose of 1 g four times daily for the duration of the period [119]. It is essential to avoid COX inhibitors due to their effect on platelet function and resulting potential to worsen bleeding [119]. In cases refractory to these options, replacement of coagulation factors may be required.

Hormonal options include combined hormonal contraceptive formulations, the LNG-IUS, and continuous systemic progestins, including injectable medroxyprogesterone acetate [119] (see section 3 for further detail), and a combination of nonhormonal and hormonal therapy is often required to provide adequate symptom relief [119].

Surgical management is appropriate where medical management has failed or a patient wishes to have definitive treatment, particularly if there is no desire for future fertility. With no other underlying pathology, the surgical treatment options are endometrial ablation or hysterectomy [119].

div.head: Ovulatory dysfunction (AUB-O)
div.p: The diagnosis of AUB-O encompasses a wide range of causes of ovulatory dysfunction, which can result in amenorrhea or manifest with irregular onset and variable menstrual volume, generally as suggested by the structured history required for FIGO System 1 [4]. The FIGO ovulatory disorders classification (HyPO-P) divides the causes into four types: Type 1 Hypothalamic, Type 2 Pituitary, Type 3 Ovarian, and Type 4 Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) [120]. Ovulatory dysfunction may occur episodically in many women or, even if chronic, may be relatively transient such as that frequently experienced in adolescence. In such instances, expectant management has a role as long as the symptoms do not adversely affect quality of life.

A detailed description of the management of ovulatory disorders is outside the scope of this article. Still, control of AUB caused by ovulatory dysfunction depends on the cause, and treatment aims to regulate cycles and provide symptom relief. The underlying cause is often endocrine, and treatment will normally involve some form of medical management [121]. Onward referral to an endocrinologist or another specialty may be indicated depending on the cause identified. Examples of treatment include levothyroxine for hypothyroidism or cabergoline to treat a prolactinoma.

Where medication adverse effects are recognized as the cause, then it is essential to consider the risks and benefits of stopping or switching treatment regimens, along with any measures that can be taken to modify unwanted adverse effects [122].

In women with ovulatory dysfunction who are overweight, weight loss and exercise should be encouraged [121,123]. Weight loss is thought to lead to a return to regular ovulation by restoring normal testosterone levels [121]. In women with PCOS, an overall weight reduction of as little as 5% may be enough to cause the spontaneous return of normal menstruation [124]. Exercise and maintenance of a healthy weight also improve quality of life and energy levels [36]. For women with hypothalamic dysfunction due to excessive exercise or low BMI, maintaining a healthy weight should be encouraged [122].

Medical management is the mainstay of treatment for AUB-O and is guided by the frequency and pattern of bleeding, contraindications to treatment, and patient preference [121]. Combined hormonal contraception (monthly, quarterly, or continuous) or progestin-only therapy can be used, which works by thinning the endometrium and protecting it from hyperplasia [2,121]. Progestin-only treatment may be in the form of the LNG-IUS, progestogen-only pill (POP), or cyclical progestogens (e.g. norethisterone [36]) (see section 3 for further detail). If a woman with PCOS has less than four menstrual periods a year, it is useful to consider periodic induction of withdrawal bleeding to protect against endometrial hyperplasia [123].

In some instances, AUB-O may be managed with endometrial ablation using the previously described techniques. Initially, it was perceived that such an approach would risk obscuring the later irregular or postmenopausal bleeding that might indicate the development of endometrial cancer or impede endometrial cavity access for diagnostic endometrial sampling. This was thought to be especially concerning in this higher-risk group. However, available evidence has not been supportive of this notion, as the overall incidence of endometrial cancer appears to be decreased compared with the untreated population [125,126]. Nevertheless, endometrial ablation in this population should still be performed in selected cases with appropriate counselling and subsequent surveillance.

div.head: Endometrial (AUB-E)
div.p: Where menstrual cycles are heavy in volume but regular and predictable in timing, and no other identifiable cause is found (including those with nonsubmucous leiomyomas), then an underlying primary disorder of the endometrium is the most likely underlying cause [76]. The mechanisms underlying the pathogenesis of AUB are described elsewhere in this Supplement (REF Jain et al.). Despite the lack of specific diagnostic tests, effective treatments for AUB-E are available, with management focused on symptom relief via medical or surgical intervention. There exists a spectrum of hormonal interventions that, in many cases, also provide effective contraception, all previously described. Consequently, the choice will consider potential contraindications to estrogens and the patient's personal preferences and previous experiences. The 52-mg LNG-IUS remains the hormonal therapy associated with the predictably greatest reduction in menstrual volume and related dysmenorrhea and one that provides highly effective contraception. If this system is unacceptable, unavailable, or contraindicated, alternative medical treatments such as combined estrogen and progestin contraception formulations or any of a spectrum of systemic progestogens can be considered.

While both progestin-only and estrogen and progestin-containing formulations may be administered cyclically, the clinician needs to understand that there is no medical reason to do so. Consequently, girls and women should be reassured that this approach has no known adverse effects, which have menstrual results similar to all of the continuous progestin interventions, including the LNG-IUS. For further information on medical therapy, see section 3.

div.head: Procedural therapy
div.p: Surgical management is indicated where medical management has failed, is contraindicated, or when a woman prefers surgical treatment, understanding that fertility will be lost [2]. Hysterectomy is the only definitive surgical treatment option for all types of AUB, but endometrial ablation is a less invasive alternative that can be used to manage AUB-E [2,41,57].

Endometrial ablation has been discussed earlier, and it should be remembered that it is an alternative to hysterectomy in women who no longer wish to conceive-the surgical goal is the destruction of the endometrium. When performed by a range of techniques, endometrial ablation is associated with an 80%-97% reduction in blood loss and rates of amenorrhea at 12 months that range from 15%-72% [127].

However, 17%-25% of women will undergo a hysterectomy or repeat ablation following the initial procedure [127], with the majority occurring in the first 2-5 years after endometrial ablation [127,128]. Despite endometrial ablation being contraindicated in women wishing to conceive in the future, the frequent preservation of some endometrium makes pregnancy a possibility, therefore patients still need effective contraception. There is a 0.7% risk of pregnancy after the procedure [16].
The overall rate of complications is 4.4% and includes hemorrhage, uterine perforation, infection, treatment failure, and postablation syndrome [16].

div.head: Iatrogenic (AUB-I)
div.p: Several medications and medical devices can cause AUB by directly affecting the endometrium, interfering with coagulation pathways, or causing ovulatory dysfunction. Most AUB-I is caused by gonadal steroid therapy. Medications that cause ovulatory dysfunction are discussed in section 4.6, but also include phenothiazines and any other agent that interferes with dopamine metabolism.
Anticoagulant drugs include warfarin, heparin, and direct oral coagulants [4].

Women using GnRH modulators may experience bleeding, especially early in the course of therapy. In particular, the estradiol flare associated with the initiation of GnRH agonist administration can cause a heavy bleed starting at about day five and potentially extending for up to 2 weeks, longer in some instances. Patients should be counselled regarding this possibility and, especially for those who are iron deficient, a 3-week course of an oral progestin (e.g. medroxyprogesterone acetate 20 mg twice per day) may mitigate or prevent the bleeding. Episodes of heavy bleeding are not associated with the initiation of GnRH antagonist therapy, but unpredictable spotting may occur that generally settles in the days and weeks following initial administration [65].
Unscheduled bleeding secondary to exogenous gonadal steroid therapy may be frequent, infrequent, prolonged, heavy, or consist of spotting or light bleeding [58].

Up to 20% of women using combined hormonal contraception will experience unscheduled bleeding [58]. The mechanisms by which such bleeding occurs are not fully understood, but evidence indicates an increase in endometrial blood vessel fragility [58]. When a patient presents in the first 3 months following the initiation of a formulation, the clinician should check compliance and medication interactions that might be contributory. Patients should be reassured that unscheduled bleeding is expected in the first 3 months and is likely to settle [58].

For AUB-I found in association with combined oral contraceptives (COCs), there may be value in switching to a different preparation or increasing the ethinyl estradiol dose to a maximum of 35 µg [58]. If these options are unacceptable, or if the unscheduled bleeding does not improve, alternative approaches to contraception or therapy should be considered.

Unscheduled bleeding with the POP is common, with 20% of users reporting prolonged bleeding [58]. It may be helpful to consider a different progestin (i.e. switching from a traditional norethindrone-containing POP to a desogestrel-based formulation) [58]. If symptoms do not improve, and while it is important to consider alternative treatment, there is no evidence to support using a double dose [58].

For the LNG-IUS or injectable progestogens such as depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA), where there are no contraindications, a short course of a COC for up to 3 months may be effective; this is usually given continuously [58]. A 5-day tranexamic and mefenamic acid trial may also be given to DMPA users to shorten the length of a bleeding episode [58]. If problematic bleeding persists, alternative treatment options should be considered. No evidence supports giving DMPA more frequently than every 3 months [Editing OK?] [58]. The bleeding pattern in the first 3 months of DMPA use likely indicates future bleeding and 20% of women will experience prolonged bleeding [58]. 4.9. Not otherwise classified (AUB-N) AUB-N includes entities that may be associated with AUB, but they are either rare, or their causal relationship has not yet been fully defined or understood [76]. This includes conditions such as chronic endometritis, arteriovenous malformations, and cesarean scar defects (also called a niche or isthmocele) [4,76]. A recently published systematic review provides convincing evidence that cesarean scar defects are not only common but, when present, the prevalence of AUB is 25.5% [129]. They often present with a distinctive bleeding pattern, which comprises some combination of prolonged menstruation and early-cycle intermenstrual bleeding [129]. Consequently, this abnormality may ultimately find a different place in FIGO's AUB System 2-the PALM-COEIN System [76].

Treatment is determined by the cause and, as with other categories, treatment decisions are dependent on patient preference and fertility plans. For example, an arteriovenous malformation may be managed by UAE or hysterectomy. An isthmocele may be amenable to hysteroscopic reshaping or excision and repair via a vaginal or abdominal approach, either laparoscopic or open [130].

div.head: Summary
div.p: Girls and women with AUB in the reproductive years present with a variety of AUB symptoms and with one or more of the potential causes defined by FIGO's PALM-COEIN system. While hysterectomy is a procedure that will successfully treat AUB symptoms agnostic of the cause, the costs, risks, and morbidity associated with this procedure are now generally unnecessary given the plethora of medical and minimally invasive procedural options available. Decisions regarding uterineconserving therapy are based on the presumed cause of the AUB, the degree of impact of the symptoms on quality of life, the patient's goals regarding future fertility, and other aspects that fall into the category of personal choice. As a result, it is incumbent on the gynecologist to offer all of the appropriate and available treatment options. Furthermore, those with the symptom of HMB are frequently adversely affected by iron deficiency, regardless of the presence or absence of anemia.
Identification and concomitant treatment of iron deficiency is an essential component of the ideal approach for girls and women with AUB in the reproductive years.

figure.figDesc: .1. Medical management The potential hormonal and nonhormonal medical interventions for AUB-E have been presented earlier in this supplement [Change to "article"?]. Tranexamic acid is perhaps the safest and most effective nonhormonal intervention, and because of its cyclical administration during menses is one that can be administered to those trying to conceive. It is unclear if the concomitant use of NSAIDs enhances the reduction in blood flow volume, but their greatest utility might be in the treatment of associated dysmenorrhea.
